loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian life insurer is presenting the firm’s capital framework to newly hired analysts. She wants one sentence on the slide that states what risk capital is for. Which of the following statements best describes the purpose of risk capital?

options.A: It is a reserve sized to the losses the insurer expects to incur on average each year, so that product pricing need not carry any loss component.
options.B: It is a cushion against unexpected losses that lets the insurer keep its financial integrity and remain a going concern even in a near-catastrophic scenario.
options.C: It is a cushion sized so that the insurer can promise its policyholders, with full certainty, that it will survive any loss over the coming year.
options.D: It is the minimum capital the insurer’s supervisor requires under industrywide formulas, set mainly to protect small policyholders from loss.

solution:
Stem summary: Canadian life insurer: one-sentence statement of the purpose of risk capital.

**Concept and theory**

Every firm faces losses that fall into two layers. The expected loss is the average loss the business generates year after year; it is a cost of doing business and is covered by pricing and reserves (for a bank, the loan loss reserve priced into the spread). The unexpected loss is the amount by which a bad year’s loss exceeds that average. Nobody can price an unexpected loss into an individual product, because it is, by construction, a deviation from the average. Something on the balance sheet has to absorb it, and that something is risk capital.

question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese bank is reviewing a training note that contrasts regulatory capital with risk capital. The note contains the following statements:

I. Regulatory capital applies only to a few regulated industries, such as banking and insurance, where regulators seek to protect small depositors or policyholders.

II. Regulatory capital is calculated from a set of industrywide rules and formulas and sets only a minimum required level of capital adequacy.

III. Because regulatory capital is calibrated to each bank’s own risk profile, the gap between a bank’s regulatory capital and its risk capital is usually narrow.

IV. If regulatory capital and risk capital are similar for the bank as a whole, they will also be similar for each of its constituent business lines.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I and II only

solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank auditor: four statements contrasting regulatory capital and risk capital.

**Concept and theory**

Risk capital is the firm’s own estimate of the cushion it needs to absorb unexpected losses at its chosen confidence level; it reflects the economic reality of the risks the firm actually runs. Regulatory capital is what a supervisor requires. GARP 18.1 warns against confusing the two and gives three contrasts:

| Dimension | Risk capital | Regulatory capital |
|---|---|---|
| Who needs it | Any firm | Only a few regulated industries (banking, insurance), to protect small depositors or policyholders |
| How computed | Firm’s own measure of its risks (VaR-type models) | Industrywide rules and formulas; sets only a minimum level of capital adequacy |

A risk consultant is sizing economic capital for the newly acquired fintech lending division of a Singapore bank. The bank defines economic capital as risk capital plus strategic risk capital, and sets risk capital at a one-year, 99.9% confidence level. The consultant gathers the following figures.

| Expected loss, one year | 60 |

| Burned-out capital spent in the start-up phase | 25 |
| Regulatory capital requirement for the division | 300 |

Economic capital = Risk capital + Strategic risk capital

question:
The treasurer of a German bank is allocating capital to two business lines. Bank-wide, regulatory capital and economic capital are both EUR 700 million, but they differ sharply by line.

| Business line | Regulatory capital (EUR m) | Economic capital (EUR m) |
|---|---|---|
| Securitization | 520 | 260 |
| Equity derivatives | 180 | 440 |
| Bank total | 700 | 700 |

The treasurer adopts the practice that some practitioners use to resolve such conflicts between the two capital measures at line level. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Securitization is charged EUR 520m and derivatives EUR 180m, and economic capital need not be computed for a line whose regulatory capital is higher.
options.B: Securitization is charged EUR 260m and derivatives EUR 180m, because each line is charged the lower of its two capital figures to avoid penalizing it.
options.C: Securitization is charged EUR 260m and derivatives EUR 440m, because the bank-wide totals agree and economic capital alone then governs the split.

Regulatory capital and economic capital can agree at the firm level and still disagree line by line, because regulatory formulas may treat an activity as riskier than management believes, or vice versa. Capital charged to line $i$ = max $\text{(RC}_{i}, \text{EC}_{i}$)

question:
A junior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is sizing risk capital for a CNY 8,000 million corporate loan book. The bank’s policy sets risk capital at a 99.9% confidence level over one year, and expected losses are priced into loan spreads. The loss model gives the following outputs.

| Loss model output (one year, % of book) | Value |
|---|---|
| Expected loss | 0.40 |
| Worst-case loss at 99% confidence | 1.60 |
| Worst-case loss at 99.9% confidence | 2.65 |

Which of the following correctly states the risk capital and its interpretation?

options.A: CNY 212 million; about a 0.1% chance over one year that losses exceed the expected loss plus this cushion.
options.B: CNY 96 million; about a 0.1% chance over one year that losses exceed the expected loss plus this cushion.
options.C: CNY 180 million; about a 0.1% chance over one year that losses exceed the expected loss plus this cushion.
options.D: CNY 180 million; no chance over one year that losses exceed the expected loss plus this cushion.

solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank loan book: risk capital at 99.9% and what it means.

**Concept and theory**

Risk capital is measured with the same concepts as VaR. Take the loss distribution over the horizon (one year). Its mean is the expected loss (EL). Pick the confidence level the firm’s policy requires; the loss at that percentile is the worst-case loss. Risk capital is the unexpected loss:

Risk capital = UL = Worst-case $\text{loss}_{c} -$ EL

where $c$ is the confidence level. EL is excluded because it is priced into the spread and reserved. The interpretation follows from $c$: at $c$ = 99.9% there is a probability of roughly 1 $- c$ = 0.1% that losses over the horizon exceed the level the firm has provided for (EL plus risk capital). No firm can offer a 100% guarantee.

question: The chief financial officer of an Australian industrial group is briefing the board. The group has two arms: a manufacturing arm funded by suppliers’ credit and bank loans, and a general insurance subsidiary that is supervised by the national insurance regulator. A director asks which capital concepts apply to which arm. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.A: Only the insurance subsidiary needs risk capital, because risk capital, like regulatory capital, is relevant only to regulated financial firms.
options.B: Both arms need risk capital to reassure their stakeholders, while regulatory capital applies only to the regulated insurance subsidiary.
options.C: Both arms need regulatory capital, because regulators protect the suppliers and lenders of industrial firms as well as policyholders.
options.D: Only the manufacturing arm needs risk capital, because the insurer’s regulatory capital already captures the true level of its risk.

solution:
Stem summary: Australian industrial group with an insurance subsidiary: which capital concepts apply to which arm.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s first contrast between risk capital and regulatory capital is about who each applies to.

- **Risk capital** is needed by any corporation: it keeps the firm a going concern and gives confidence to its stakeholders. For an industrial firm these are suppliers, clients and lenders; for a financial institution, claimholders such as depositors and counterparties.
- **Regulatory capital** applies only to a few regulated industries, such as banking and insurance companies, where regulators are trying to protect the interests of small depositors or policyholders. It is set by industrywide rules and rarely captures the true level of risk.

question: A treasury analyst at a German Landesbank is presenting the bank’s new risk-adjusted performance framework to newly hired analysts. She wants one slide that explains how RAROC improves on accounting measures such as return on book equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA). Which statement should she put on the slide?

options.A: RAROC deducts expected loss from the return in the numerator and replaces accounting capital with economic capital in the denominator.
options.B: RAROC leaves net income unadjusted in the numerator and replaces accounting capital with economic capital in the denominator.
options.C: RAROC adds expected loss back to the return in the numerator and replaces accounting capital with economic capital in the denominator.
options.D: RAROC deducts expected loss from the return in the numerator and replaces accounting capital with risk-adjusted assets in the denominator.

solution:
Stem summary: Treasury analyst at a Landesbank choosing the slide that says how RAROC improves on ROE and ROA.

**Concept and theory**

Traditional accounting measures of performance, such as return on assets (ROA) and return on book equity (ROE), fail to capture the risk of the underlying activity. Book assets and book equity are accounting quantities and are poor proxies for risk, and accounting income misses critical risk adjustments, most importantly expected loss. Two units can show the same ROE while one of them is running far more risk.

RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital), first proposed by Bankers Trust in the late 1970s, fixes both halves of the ratio:

RAROC = $\frac{\text{after-tax expected risk-adjusted net income}}{\text{economic capital}}$

III. The return on risk capital is the return earned by investing the allocated risk capital at the bank’s cost of equity.

IV. Transfers cover only the funding charge levied by the treasury group; head office overhead allocations belong in direct costs.

where ∆EL is the change in expected loss in currency units, $t$ the effective tax rate and EC economic capital.

question:
A regulator at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is reviewing how a bank builds the denominator of its RAROC. The bank’s methodology paper makes the following statements:

I. Economic capital can be defined as risk capital plus strategic risk capital, where strategic risk capital is the sum of goodwill and burned-out capital.

II. Burned-out capital is amortized over time as the risk of strategic failure of the initiative dissipates.

III. Risk capital equals the worst-case loss at the chosen confidence level, including the expected loss of the activity.

IV. Risk capital may be allocated to unused risk limits, such as undrawn credit lines, because that capacity can be tapped at any moment.

solution:
Stem summary: HKMA regulator reviewing four statements on how a bank builds the RAROC denominator.

**Concept and theory**

GARP builds the RAROC denominator in layers:

- **Risk capital:** the cushion against the worst-case loss minus the expected loss from market, credit, operational and other risks (business, reputation) at the required confidence level, directly related to one-year VaR.
- **Strategic risk capital:** for significant investments of highly uncertain success. Current practice measures it as burned-out capital plus goodwill.
